entries.title: Tundu Lissu: After escaping the death penalty, what does his guilty verdict mean for Tanzania's democracy?
entries.summary: A treason trial could have meant death by hanging for Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu. Instead, he now faces four years in prison for incitement to unrest. Ban dissident voices truly be heard in the country?
entries.content:
Tanzania

Tundu Lissu verdict: What does it mean for Tanzania's democracy?

November 11, 2026

A treason trial could have meant death by hanging for Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu. Instead, he now faces four years in prison for incitement to unrest. Ban dissident voices truly be heard in the country?

On November 6, Tundu Lissu, leader of Tanzania's main opposition Chadema party, was sentenced to four years in prison for incitement following heavy unrest during the October 2025 elections.

The same day, he was cleared of treason charges — which could have meant a death sentence if he had been found guilty.

Lissu commented that the judiciary had acted under pressure; he rejected the verdict due to the fact that incitement was not among the charges which had brought against him at the start of his trial in 2025.

Chadema officials have now signaled an intention to appeal the court decision. The government has not issued a statement on his conviction yet.

Tanzania's most dramatic trial in decades

Few opposition figures have shaped modern Tanzanian politics as dramatically as Lissu. A lawyer by training and one of the country's most outspoken critics of the ruling party Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM), Lissu has spent years challenging the political establishment.

Over the years, he has been subjected to repeated arrest and detention; in 2017, he survived an attempt on his life by unknown gunmen outside his residence in the capital Dodoma, sustaining multiple bullet wounds.

More recently, his trial in the run-up to the October 2025 general election continued to keep him and the opposition in the public eye following his arrest in April 2025 in the southwestern town of Mbinga.

Why was Tundu Lissu arrested?

Prosecuters accused Lissu of encouraging the public to prevent the 2025 election from taking place and charged him with one count of treason.

As legal evidence, they cited social media posts he had made, in which he was seen to be calling on Tanzanians to boycott the vote over concerns about possible electoral malpractice.

In the end, the election went ahead without Chadema on October 29, which was marred by violence on an unprecedented in scale in Tanzania; security forces even used live ammunition on protesters.

Francis Ibrahim, an independent political analyst based in Dar es Salaam, told DW that "heads have to roll from the law enforcement side, who overstretched their mandate, all the way to the people, who financed, planned and organized [this crackdown]."

But after a nationwide internet shutdown and curfew following the election violence, incumbent President Samia Suluhu Hassan was named winner with 98% of the vote.

What does the verdict mean for democracy?

Ibrahim believes that the removal of the capital treason charge could be interpreted as a move towards rapprochment with voters.

"What I can tell you is that they are looking for a political deescalation that could solve the crisis," he explained, adding that Lissu might yet get to have a small say in politics after all:

"There has to be a process of [creating] a new constitution, and it needs everybody on the table," he said, adding that Lissu might therefore perhaps be released early in order to partake in discussions and negotiations.

However when in late July, President Suluhu Hassan met with representatives of more than a dozen political parties to discuss national reconciliation and constitutional reform, Chadema officials were explicitly not party to the consultations.

Politics at play behind the verdict?

Public opinion meanwhile varies on Lissu's verdict, with many Tanzanians however saying that the trial was politically motivated in their view.

Ruqaya Mohammed, the National Deputy Secretary of the oppsition ACT-Wazalendo party's youth wing, told DW, "ee are getting into a darker space in our political arena."

"I think it's the right time now, as a nation, to have open dialogue on some reforms, on the legal perspective and electoral reforms. Maybe if we manage ... that, we can see a light," she explained.

Most others, however, remain reluctant to go on record for fear of reprisal; a musician and human rights advocate was among few who agreed to speak to DW — on the strict condition of anonymity.

In his view, Tanzanians simply are not free to express themselves publicly at all: "You saw the terror atmosphere and climate of fear outside the court premises when Tundu's judgement was ... read. Such is the broader display of what Tanzania looks like," he told DW. 

"Opposition politics has been suppressed for years, and his conviction is just a continuation of what has been happening. It's a miracle that he is still alive. To put him in jail from four years is far from the worst-case scenario."

This article has been adapted from an episode of DW's AfricaLink podcast.

entries.title: Germany news: Only 1/3 of Germans satisfied with state of democracy
entries.summary: A new authoritarianism study has revealed a new low in satisfaction levels with the functioning of German democracy. Meanwhile, the Bundeswehr has banned Chinese-made drones. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Only 1/3 of Germans satisfied with state of democracy

Published November 11, 2026last updated November 11, 2026

A new authoritarianism study has revealed a new low in satisfaction levels with the functioning of German democracy. Meanwhile, the Bundeswehr has banned Chinese-made drones. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • New study reveals record low satisfaction with democracy in Germany
  • Data has revealed that workers aged 60-65 take an average of 31.3 sick days off a year
  • Carneval season festivities are kicking
  • Inflation has dipped below 3% thanks to the fuel rebate
  • The German military has banned the use of Chinese-made drones

Keep reading for the top news and analysis from Germany on Wednesday, November 11:

Skip next section German female soldiers report widespread harassment

German female soldiers report widespread harassment

The German Bundeswehr has a sexual harassment problem, especially for its female soldiers, according to the results of a survey released by the Defense Ministry on Wednesday.

The data revealed that 38% of female soldiers had been subject to sexualized verbal harassment in the past 12 months. For male soldiers, the share was 16%.

Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said that female, young and non-heterosexual soldiers suffered the most from sexualized harassment. He outlined a plan to address the issue, saying: "Zero tolerance applies to sexual harassment within the Bundeswehr."

Some 7% of female soldiers said pictures of them had been taken without consent or edited with AI. Another 9% reported physical sexual assault and 2% reported being victim to sexualized violence.

For male soldiers, 2% also reported being subject to sexualized violence in the Bundeswehr.

Depending on the type of harassment, between 36% and 61% said they had not reported incidents, citing fear of consequences. Between 44% and 59% said they were doubtful the reporting would lead to anything.

The results of the study, which Pistorius called the "very first of its kind," were based on 8,000 filled out questionnaires. That represents 4% of the Bundeswehr's 186,200 total military personnel.

The German government is seeking to boost the numbers of the Bundeswehr to 260,000 active members with 200,000 reservists. This requires attracting both men and women into the forces.

Skip next section Satisfaction with democracy in Germany reaches new low — study

Satisfaction with democracy in Germany reaches new low — study

Just a third of respondents said they were satisfied with the state of democracy in the Federal Republic of Germany, according to a new report from the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study.

This marked a steep decline from the 42.3% level of satisfaction measured in the last study in 2024 and was the lowest point since the study began in 2002. The level was even lower in the former East German states where only 22.8% expressed satisfaction with German democracy, down from 29.7%.

At the same time, 89.3% of respondents said they agreed with the concept of democracy, however, this also marked the first time this level fell below 90%.

A large share of respondents also expressed chauvinistic and antisemitic views.

In response to the statement "Germany is being dangerously overrun by foreigners," 34.9% were manifestly in agreement, with 24.4% in latent agreement.

At the same time, 15.5% manifestly agreed with the statement "the influence of Jews in Germany is still too great," with 21.7% latently agreeing.

The research was carried out by the Else-Frenkel-Brunswik-Institut at the University of Leipzig. They surveyed 2,500 people between mid-March and the beginning of June this year.

Skip next section IN PICTURES: New South America exhibit opens in Hamburg's Miniatur Wunderland

IN PICTURES: New South America exhibit opens in Hamburg's Miniatur Wunderland

Skip next section Bundeswehr to stop using Chinese-made drones

Bundeswehr to stop using Chinese-made drones

The German military, or Bundeswehr, has said it had banned the use of Chinese-made drones, the Defense Ministry said.

The ban also includes for training purposes. Instead, the military can use German or European-made drones.

The ministry cited "security-relevant information," saying "Chinese-made models will no longer be used ... and existing systems will be replaced by products from domestic or, where applicable, European sources."

The Bundeswehr may purchase "inexpensive, off-the-shelf drones for training purposes", buying them "with minimal bureaucratic effort."

Skip next section Suspect in death of 13-year-old girl dies in hospital

Suspect in death of 13-year-old girl dies in hospital

A 22-year-old man has died in hospital from severe head injuries after he was found by police in an abandoned building with the body of a 13-year-old girl who had gone missing.

The man tried to shoot himself after being discovered by police in the small town of Altglietzen on the border with Poland on Sunday. He sustained life-threatening injuries and was taken to hospital for intensive care.

Prosecutors in Berlin said on Monday that the man had already been under investigation since January 2025 amid suspicion of possession of child sexual abuse material.

The 13-year-old victim went missing Tuesday last week after she left her home in Berlin at 7:15 a.m. to go to school. She never arrived.

Skip next section WATCH: Autonomous drones — rescuers from above?

WATCH: Autonomous drones — rescuers from above?

Autonomous drones can navigate without GPS, search for missing persons and make decisions on their own.

In Germany, developers competed to see which drone was the best rescuer.

Skip next section Carneval festivities to begin in Cologne despite inclement weather

Carneval festivities to begin in Cologne despite inclement weather

Rain has not appeared to put off carneval-revellers in Cologne with festivities set to kick off at 11:11 a.m. (1011 GMT) on November 11.

Groups of people in colorful costumes had already started gathering outside the Cologne main station, at the foot of the famous Cologne Cathedral, despite the wet weather.

Bakeries have been selling their traditional carneval pastries like hot cakes.

Local authorities expect tens of thousands of people to join the celebrations. Some 1,000 police officers as well as 1,200 agents from a private security firm have been deployed.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Germany's climate standing sinks to lowest level in years

IN DEPTH: Germany's climate standing sinks to lowest level in years

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Columbia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Skip next section October inflation falls below 3% amid fuel rebate

October inflation falls below 3% amid fuel rebate

Year-on-year inflation for October dropped down slightly to 2.8% after reaching 3.3% in September, according to preliminary figures from the Federal Office of Statistics (Destatis).

Record high prices for gas and diesel pushed up inflation in September but this was brought down thanks to government subsidy for consumers at the gas pump that was introduced in October.

"The main factor behind the persistently high inflation rate remained the trend in energy prices, even though the fuel subsidy, which was reintroduced in early October, may have tempered inflation somewhat," Destatis President Ruth Brand said.

Skip next section Workers over 60 taking a month off per year for sick leave

Workers over 60 taking a month off per year for sick leave

German workers aged between 60 and 65 took an average of 31.3 days of sick leave per year, based on data from 2024 released by the Health Ministry in response to a question posed by the Left party in the Bundestag.

The average number of sick days taken by all workers was 15, according to the Federal Office of Statistics (Destatis).

The number of 60 to 65-year-olds who have taken a year or more off for sick leave has also increased in recent years. It went from around 80,300 people in 2022 to 96,100 in 2024.

Left party spokesperson Sarah Vollath called the figures a "clear warning sign" in comments to the Rheinische Post and warned that workers cannot "keep working forever."

"If the federal government has its way, the retirement age for workers will soon be pushed even further into the future due to another increase in the standard retirement age. This completely ignores the reality of life for older workers."

The government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz has set retirement reform as one of its main goals, with policies including pushing the retirement age back to 67 years.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning and Alaaf!

November 11, as well as being Armistice Day, is also the first day of the carneval season with events taking place throughout the Rhineland region, including in Cologne, Düsseldorf and Mainz.

We are also expecting the German Council of Economic Experts to publish their annual report providing forecasts and proposals to the German government.

Keep reading for this and more.

entries.title: Iran classes Argentina navy, air force as 'terrorist organizations'
entries.summary: In a tit-for-tat move, Iran has said it now considers Argentina's navy and air force as "terrorist organizations." Tehran claimed Buenos Aires is responsible for further consequences.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran classes Argentina navy, air force as 'terrorist organizations'

November 11, 2026

In a tit-for-tat move, Iran has said it now considers Argentina's navy and air force as "terrorist organizations." Tehran claimed Buenos Aires is responsible for further consequences.

Iran's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday that it classified Argentina's navy and air force as "terrorist organizations."

In early April, Argentina designated Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a "terrorist organization," as US President Donald Trump pressured his allies to do so following the war on Iran.

Tehran's designation came "based on the principle of reciprocity," Iran's ​Foreign ‌Ministry said in a statement.

"It is ‌evident ​that the responsibility for all consequences arising from this matter will lie with the Argentine government," the ministry added, ​without a mention of Argentina's army.

Iran passed a legislation in 2019 that grants retaliatory measures against states that designate its military as a terrorist group.

Argentina holds Hezbollah responsible for deadly attacks

Argentina said in April that it had taken action against the IRGC because of its support for the Lebanon-based militant group Hezbollah.

Buenos Aires holds Hezbollah responsible for the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community center, which killed 85 people.

IRGC classified as a terrorist group by many countries

IRGC was established at the end of Iran's 1979 Islamic Revolution as an elite armed militia whose role was to protect the then embryonic Shiite clerical regime.

Over the years, it has morphed into a vast economic and political empire. Rather than the elected president, the force answers directly to Iran's supreme leader.

The United States, the European Union, and the United Kingdom, along with other countries, classify the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist organization.

entries.title: Spain: Housing crisis prompts general strike
entries.summary: Workers across nearly all industries have taken to the picket lines as rents soar and the housing crunch worsens. The crisis is the main political debate ahead of Spain's November 29 elections.
entries.content:
Spain

Spain: Housing crisis prompts general strike

November 11, 2026

Workers across nearly all industries have taken to the picket lines as rents soar and the housing crunch worsens. The crisis is the main political debate ahead of Spain's November 29 elections.

Workers across Spain gathered en mass on Wednesday, marching and setting up picket lines despite stormy weather in many areas of the country.

This is the first general strike in Spain in 14 years, amid a worsening cost of living and lack of housing crisis that has left many unable to support themselves.

Symbolized by the eviction and death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in Madrid earlier this year, the crisis has also prompted a snap election set for November 29.

The government of left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez attempted to pass legislation to ease the plight of renters, but was blocked in parliament by opposition parties. Lacking the power to get legislation passed, Sanchez called the early vote in hopes to shore up more support.

"We won't stop until we transform this country's housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the [landlord] minority," said Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union.

While most of the protests appeared to be proceeding peacefully, strikers in front of Madrid's Mercamadrid wholesale market said that police had used pepper spray on the crowd, prompting at least 13 people to seek medical attention.

Some airlines later reported disruptions on flights in and out of Spain as some airport and airline workers participated in the strike.

How bad is Spain's housing crisis?

The country has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set ​to grow to more than a million by 2028 according to estimates from the central bank.

With fewer and fewer individuals and families able to buy a home, the number of renters in the country has risen sharply. According to Spain's youth council, the average rent is €1,176 ($1,315). This is equivalent to 99% of the average young person's salary.

The general strike comes a day after rail workers launched a strike over two major deadly train crashes this year, making decrepit infrastructure also a major topic in the upcoming parliamentary elections.

How have political leaders reacted to the strike?

The government has support the strike, saying it is being held "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition."

Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP), stated that if this is indeed "a strike against the opposition," it is "an absurdity the likes of which does not exist in any other European Union country."

Although the UGT labor union, one of the organizers of the strike, and Sanchez's socialist PSOE party are two separate institutions, they do share a historic founder in Pablo Iglesias Posse.

Strike supported by sitting government, many in Spain believe

Nicole Ras, reporting for DW in Madrid, has been following the strike closely as it unfolds on Wednesday. Here's what she has to say:

Here in Madrid apparently lots of people are still showing up for work and people I know have clearly said they will not go on strike as they don't see much sense in it (although they all suffer under the cost living crisis and the housing crisis).

"I'm not taking part in this. It's nonsense. The government is supporting it because they hope they'll get enough votes on the 29th so they can carry on," a doorman in Madrid told me.

There is also a debate about this strike being an "election strike" that could benefit the current government.

The government supports the strike, claiming it is being held "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez's inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition," according to the media here.

entries.title: DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.
entries.summary: Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

Be bored: Why you should schedule time to do nothing

November 11, 2026

Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Your brain has its own version of that.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

An accidental find: The discovery of the default mode network

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

What does the default mode network do?

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

How your brain switches from DMN to focus on external tasks

There's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?"

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

But it's not an on/off switch.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

Smartphones and the brain: Are we crowding out boredom?

Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

The dark side of the DMN: Rumination, depression and Alzheimer's

The DMN is not always necessarily good.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great new idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

How to protect your brain's default mode network

Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Embrace boredom and enjoy doing nothing.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

entries.title: India: CPCB addresses stark Delhi pollution data gap on Diwali night
entries.summary: India's main pollution monitor has issued a clarification on a wide air quality data gap between official and private reporting in New Delhi that saw the city choked amid Diwali fireworks. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
India

India: CPCB addresses stark Delhi pollution data gap on Diwali night

Published November 11, 2026last updated November 11, 2026

India's main pollution monitor has issued a clarification on a wide air quality data gap between official and private reporting in New Delhi that saw the city choked amid Diwali fireworks. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Following are the latest developments from Indian on Wednesday, November 11

  • India's anti-pollution watchdog said its analyzers are calibrated to measure particulate matter only within a specified range
  • The CPCB said its air quality monitoring methodology is under review
  • India and France discuss cooperation in space, critical technology and economic security

Skip next section WATCH — Online gambling fuels debt, addiction worries in India

WATCH — Online gambling fuels debt, addiction worries in India

India's booming online betting market is drawing millions of users with the promise of quick wins, but experts warn the social and financial costs can be severe.

As cheap mobile internet and digital payments make online gambling more accessible across the country, concerns are growing about debt, addiction and the challenges facing families affected by gambling losses.

The issue has become a major test for regulators, who are struggling to curb illegal betting platforms that can quickly reappear under new domains. Meanwhile, rehabilitation centers have reported rising numbers of young people seeking help for gambling addiction.

As India attempts to regulate a fast-evolving digital gambling industry, questions remain over enforcement, public awareness and support for those caught in the cycle of online betting.

Find out more in this report:

Skip next section India and France talk cooperation in space, critical technologies

India and France talk cooperation in space, critical technologies

India and France have discussed enhancing cooperation in sectors like space, critical technologies, cybersecurity and industrial partnerships, India's foreign ministry said late Tuesday.

India's Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri was in Paris, co-chairing two bilateral forums with the Secretary-General of the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Martin Briens.

The two sides talked about the existing bilateral engagement in the space sector at the 3rd India-France Strategic Space Dialogue and discussed prospects for further cooperation in government-to-government and commercial segments, New Delhi said.

Tuesday also saw the inaugural meeting of the India-France Economic Security and Critical Technologies Dialogue, which was established during  Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to France in June this year. 

Discussion between Misri and Briens at the forum, focused on supply chain vulnerabilities, critical technologies, cybersecurity and safeguarding strategic supplies, the Indian foreign ministry said.

"Both sides agreed to work on the priorities identified during the dialogue," it added.

The officials also held diplomatic consultations to review the entire spectrum of India-France bilateral ties. 

India said Misri's France visit reflected "the continued regular high-level exchanges” between the two countries and “the shared commitment of both sides to further deepen their Special Global Strategic Partnership."

Skip next section Air India plane moved to isolation bay in Kolkata after hijack alert

Air India plane moved to isolation bay in Kolkata after hijack alert

An Air India flight was isolated at West Bengal's Kolkata airport on Wednesday afternoon shortly before its scheduled takeoff, following a hijack alert, Indian media reports said.

"The incident has occurred on Air India flight AI 772. For safety reasons, the aircraft has been moved to an isolation bay. Security personnel have rushed to the spot and surrounded the entire aircraft to begin a thorough search," The Indian Express cited an official as saying.

According to reports, the aircraft was preparing to take off from Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International (NSCBI) Airport for Mumbai when cabin crew members noticed a hijack alert written on the mirror of one of the plane's lavatories.

The pilot immediately sounded an alert to the Air Traffic Control, NDTV reported.

The passengers were deplaned, Hindustan Times reported, citing an airport police officer.

Reports said that security agencies were probing the incident.

"Necessary checks are currently underway by the concerned agencies in accordance with established protocols," news agency ANI quoted a statement from the airport as saying.

Skip next section Four injured as five coaches of train derail in Assam

Four injured as five coaches of train derail in Assam

Five coaches and the engine of a passenger train derailed in the state of Assam, leaving four people injured, according to local reports on Wednesday. 

The accident occurred around 6.54 am local time and involved the Kolkata-Sairang Express.

The train was being received at Digaru railway station when the locomotive tried to let another train pass and its driver "could not control" the speed, a statement from Northeast Frontier Railway said.

The incident resulted in the derailment of the coaches, the statement added, initially reporting no injuries.

However, Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma later said four people had suffered minor injuries and were receiving care.

"All passengers are safe," Sarma wrote on X.

He added that basic necessities were being given to stranded passengers and that an alternative train had been arranged for their journey.

A recovery train was also deployed to the spot for rescue operations and clearance of the tracks, news agency PTI cited a railway official as saying.

Skip next section Delhi air pollution: Central body says air quality data gap due to methodology 'differences' not 'underreporting'

Delhi air pollution: Central body says air quality data gap due to methodology 'differences' not 'underreporting'

India's Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has issued a clarification on data gap concerns in New Delhi after pollution monitoring in the capital came under scrutiny on Diwali night with official data showing a much lower Air Quality Index (AQI) than private platforms and reports saying that several of the city's monitoring stations went blank. 

Celebrations during the Hindu festival of Diwali on Sunday blanketed New Delhi and other surrounding areas in a dense and toxic smog as revelers defied a firecracker ban, adding to the region's seasonal pollution woes. 

As smoke and particulate matter from the fireworks kept being released into Delhi's air, an alarmingly wide difference was seen in air pollution figures between official government data and the numbers on private websites and applications.

The CPCB's app showed the AQI at 400 on Diwali night while numbers on private platforms breached the 2,000 mark.

The difference in AQI values was "attributable to differences in measurement of pollutant concentration and in methodology, and not to underreporting," the CPCB said in a statement on X, published Tuesday night.

The anti-pollution watchdog further added that analyzers under its National Air Quality Index (NAQI) reporting methodology, introduced in 2015, were calibrated to measure particulate matter levels of only up to 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre.

Air quality monitors blackout

Indian media outlets this week reported that several of the capital's 59 to 60 air pollution monitoring stations went dark on the festival of lights and stopped giving data, when pollution was at its peak in the night.

The Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), one of the agencies that operate the capital's monitoring stations, later released the missing data which showed one area of the city witnessing an hourly PM 2.5 concentration of 3,744 micrograms per cubic metre late on Diwali night.

The level was 60 times the national average but CPCB said the readings were not used to calculate the AQI as "the designed system of automated data validation treats hourly readings beyond the calibrated range as outside range."

"During extreme episodes, which are occasional like Diwali firecracker bursting, this may appear as a data gap at the particular station concerned, and those hours do not contribute to the 24-hour average of relevant pollutant for concerned station," the body said.

The CPCB went on to say that it is reviewing its existing methodology, considering the advancements in monitoring technology and international practice.

"Internal deliberations and consultations with respect to processing of data beyond system design range are underway," it said.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

I am Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's bureau in New Delhi and this is the Wednesday edition of our India wrap. Here we breakdown all the biggest headlines that are making a splash in the world's most populous nation.

India's central pollution body has released a statement addressing concerns around a reported data gap in air quality monitoring as Diwali fireworks over the weekend left the capital choking on toxic smog.

In other news, several people are reported to have been injured in a trail derailment in the state of Assam.

And in developments from the world of diplomacy, India and France have discussed enhancing cooperation in critical technologies and cybersecurity.

Stay with us as we bring you all this and more.

entries.title: Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains
entries.summary: Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.
entries.content:
November 11, 2026

Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate plans, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy."

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

"We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum."

That momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," said CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

G20 countries perform particularly poorly

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey said Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

The G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low."

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China a renewable leader but has the world's highest emissions

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

However, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, said the report.

The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action."

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: How AI worsens online violence against Middle East women
entries.summary: Women in the Middle East already have to deal with an above-average share of online harassment and violence. The proliferation of AI-enabled tools is making it worse.
entries.content:
Middle East

How AI worsens online violence against Middle East women

November 11, 2026

Women in the Middle East already have to deal with an above-average share of online harassment and violence. The proliferation of AI-enabled tools is making it worse.

It happens all the time, says Kholoud al-Ameri, an Iraqi journalist and the editor of a news website.

"Female journalists here are often getting messages, and mostly from men," she explains. "They somehow find you online and then they say they just want to talk or they want to add you on Instagram or Facebook," says al-Ameri, who also heads a network of female journalists working on climate change stories. "Sometimes it's hard because the men say they're our readers and we don't want to discourage them. But I usually tell the women just to block these guys."

Syrian activist Yaman Amer tells of similar experiences as a result of writing about women's rights online — she says she gets hundreds of critical comments. "When I talk about women's rights online in a patriarchal society, that's just how things are," Amer, who is studying to be a lawyer in Damascus, told DW. "Not that I accept it. Out of every thousand offensive comments, there's usually one or two that make me feel like I have to report them because they're particularly vile. As in, they're extremely vulgar or threatening. And then it's more than just harassment. It's on a whole other level, humiliating and degrading."

Above-average abuse

Online harassment of women isn't unusual anywhere. Studies by a variety of organizations show that somewhere between 40% and 60% of all women worldwide have experienced it, while 65% have witnessed it.

There is no single standard for assessing the level of online harassment because surveys often use different types of questions or research methods. But in general, women around the Middle East appear to be dealing with a higher-than-global-average level of what is known as "technology facilitated gender-based violence," or TFGBV.

The United Nations Population Fund defines TFGBV as a harmful act "that is committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified ... by the use of information communication technologies," or other digital tools, "against a person on the basis of their gender."

According to research by UN Women, the UN body dedicated to gender equality, 68% of women in the Middle East have had to deal with it, while almost all — close to 100% — have seen it online.

In a 2025 study, UN Women found that 49% of women using the internet in the Middle East don't feel safe from online harassment. The number goes up to almost 70% if the women are more publicly visible activists, journalists or politicians.

And it is already clear that the increased availability of artificial intelligence-powered applications is making online harassment worse.

AI has the potential to supercharge this kind of abuse, the UN Women briefing points out, "both by facilitating the spread of targeted disinformation as well as the proliferation of image-based abuse and deepfake pornographic videos."

Of the women who had experienced online violence while working, around a quarter had already identified "abuse that was generated or amplified by AI tools," the briefing said.

AI makes abuse easier

The potential for using the latest technology in order to harass people online has always been there, says Siddharth Venkataramakrishnan, an analyst at the London-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), which investigates extremism. "But it's just become easier to produce harmful content at scale and in a hyper-targeted way. And the production of non-consensual imagery is a real marker of the democratization of that technology, so it's moving away from primarily targeting celebrities to just regular people."

Venkataramakrishnan has been researching incidents that occurred at the beginning of 2026 when Grok, the AI-powered chatbot belonging to Elon Musk's company SpaceXAI, became able to alter photographs to depict a fully dressed subject as nearly naked. The scandal caused Grok's services to be restricted but, as Venkataramakrishnan pointed out, safeguards across different AI models tend to be inconsistent and users can still find work-arounds to get similar results.

In conservative cultures in the Middle East, the threat of this kind of half-naked picture of a woman being published has serious real-life implications, mostly because of what is and isn't acceptable for women around the region.

What makes the increase in AI-generated fakes even more problematic in the Middle East is that online abuse also has a higher chance of having offline effects.

"Norms related to honor, family reputation and male control can turn digital abuse into real-world consequences," a June briefing by the World Bank notes.

Lack of specific laws

It's also often not easy for people targeted with this kind of abuse to find legal protection or even somewhere to report it. While some Middle Eastern countries have cybercrime laws, most don't specifically address gender-based online violence nor have they been updated to grapple with AI-related abuse.

Last year's UN Women survey found that 36% of women said they were just told to ignore the online violence, while 23% were blamed for it themselves and 12% were subjected to physical punishment by their families because of it.

Other studies indicate that only about 7% of women who experienced technology-facilitated violence later report it to law enforcement. Various concerns stop them from doing so, including having to present sexualized images or answer personal questions in front of strangers — often also anathema to many women in the region.

The women who had experienced online harassment said they would often just block the perpetrators and around a quarter said they then became more careful about what they posted online. Twenty percent deleted their accounts or left social media altogether.

Conflict situations

The rapid growth in AI-enabled harassment can also be more problematic in the Middle East because of the situations the women targeted find themselves living in.

Displacement, war, conflict and instability can all make women more vulnerable to online abuse and exploitation. Even the rapid development of AI-related technologies in a country without corresponding legal guardrails or digital literacy can increase the risk.

For example, observers point out that Saudi Arabia, a generally conservative country with strict rules for female behavior, is going through an accelerated program of digital transformation.

And in Syria, after the ousting of the dictatorial Assad regime, many Syrians "rushed into social media to speak freely," journalist Zaina Erhaim wrote for the Arab Reform Initiative in July this year.

Previously. digital polices had been closely policed by Syria's dictator and a political post could see the writer thrown in jail. But now Syrians "are navigating this newfound liberty without guardrails, oversight or protection," Erhaim argues, and female activists are paying a high price for it, especially where "gender intersects with sect."

In a policy paper published in May, the Syrian Women's Political Movement explained just how bad online abuse had become. In focus groups with 120 women from all around Syria, the majority of participants agreed that digital abuse had become a way of shutting them up. Younger activists reported personal pictures were being stolen from social media, then used against them.

"Smear campaigns targeting women's 'honor' and systemic defamation are actively deployed as punitive measures against any women who attempt to express a critical political opinion," the organization wrote, arguing that what was needed was a law that criminalized digital violence.

If you or someone you know have experienced any kind of gender-based violence, the website lila.help (https://lila.help) lists trustworthy helplines and NGOs that offer support in almost every country around the world.

entries.title: South Korea bus causes large crash near Seoul, dozens hurt
entries.summary: The bus triggered a collision involving more than 30 vehicles, including other buses, during rush hour traffic in the South Korean city of Seongnam, just south of Seoul.
entries.content:
South Korea

South Korea bus causes large crash near Seoul, dozens hurt

November 11, 2026

The bus triggered a collision involving more than 30 vehicles, including other buses, during rush hour traffic in the South Korean city of Seongnam, just south of Seoul.

A bus triggered a crash involving dozens of passenger cars, a truck, and four other buses in Seongnam, South Korea on Wednesday morning, leaving many injured, according to South Korean authorities. 

What do we know so far?

The fire department of Gyeonggi Province, were Seongnam is located, said 57 people were injured, with nine seriously hurt after the bus initiated a crash involving 32 vehicles and then slammed into a median strip. None of the injured were in life-threatening condition. Yonhap News Agency had reported that 48 people were injured and six of them had serious injuries.

An investigation has been launched into the cause of the collision.

The driver told investigators the brakes on his bus had failed, according to a report by Yonhap news agency. The man, believed to be in his 60s, tested negative in a breathalyzer test. Local media had reported that he was also hospitalized after the crash.

The city of Seongnam, with its population of nearly 900,000, is located just south of the capital metropolis of Seoul. The crash occurred during rush hour traffic.

Dozens of fire personnel and vehicles were deployed to the scene of the crash and a emergency medical station was also set up there.

entries.title: Israel: Eisenkot proposes October 7 probe as new Knesset sworn in
entries.summary: Ex-IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot has yet to forge a coalition that would allow him to replace Benjamin Netanyahu, despite the new Knesset being dominated by the critics of the current prime minister.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel: Eisenkot proposes October 7 probe as new Knesset sworn in

November 11, 2026

Ex-IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot has yet to forge a coalition that would allow him to replace Benjamin Netanyahu, despite the new Knesset being dominated by the critics of the current prime minister.

The parliamentary bloc led by Israeli ex-military leader Gadi Eisenkot announced a slew of initiatives on Tuesday targeting the legacy of current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as the new Israeli Parliament, or Knesset, was sworn in.

Israel held a parliamentary election on October 27. 

Eisenkot's bloc wants government inquiry into October 7 attack

Eisenkot's centrist Yashar Party and allied parties are seeking an official government inquiry into the Hamas-led terror attacks on October 7, 2023, which killed some 1,200 people in Israel and resulted in another 251 hostages being taken into Gaza.

The attack, which occurred on Netanyahu's watch, was the single deadliest day for Jewish people since the Holocaust.

Some media outlets had reported that Netanyahu received warnings from Egypt and the UAE ahead of the October 7 assault. The Israeli prime minister denied the claims and said he would sue for defamation over the publications. 

In addition to an October 7 probe, the anti-Netanyahu opposition is also seeking to impose term limits on the office of prime minister and aims to reverse the controversial efforts made by the Netanyahu government to reforming the judiciary.  Eisenkot's bloc is also seeking to depose Knesset speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally. 

"We will act for all citizens of Israel, those who voted for us and those who did not, out of deep commitment," Eisenkot said prior to the swearing-in of the new Knesset. He pledged to "form a national-emergency government as quickly as possible."

Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot bloc short of Knesset majority

Israeli President Isaac Herzog has given Eisenkot a mandate to try to form a government within six weeks. 

Eisenkot's coalition bloc landed 48 seats in the recent election, whereas Netanyahu's bloc received 53 seats. But neither bloc has enough seats to form a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

Arab parties garnered a record 19 out of 120 seats in the new Knesset. During the swearing-in ceremony, far-right Israeli politician Itamar Ben-Gvir harassed Arab-Israeli lawmaker Yousef Jabareen in the Knesset chamber

Eisenkot's bloc could choose to align with the Arab parties to form a government, but Avigdor Lieberman and his right-wing Yisrael Beitenu party oppose the idea. Yisrael Beitenu, which won seven seats in the new Knesset, is a part of the Eisenkot bloc.

Netanyahu urges national unity government to confront Iran

Netanyahu, in a speech to the Knesset, called for a national unity government — a proposal which has been ruled out by Eisenkot. The incumbent head of government lashed out at Arab parties and accused them of backing Israel's destruction while saying the national unity government is necessary to confront Iran. 

"In the very near future, we're going to be confronted by international pressure to accept a nuclear-armed Iran and the preservation of this terror regime that seeks to annihilate us," Netanyahu said.

Eisenkot condemned Netanyahu's remarks, whereas Yair Golan, the leader of the left-wing Democrats party, walked out during Netanyahu's speech. The Democrats have eight seats and are part of the Eisenkot bloc.

"Netanyahu is struggling to accept that the Israeli public fired him. Now he is lying and inciting against the Arab public in an attempt to cling to power by force," Golan said on X.

If Eisenkot fails to form a government, Israeli President Herzog could choose another lawmaker, presumably Netanyahu, to cobble together a coalition. The 77-year-old Netanyahu first took power in 1996 and has had three separate stints as the Israeli head of government.

Netanyahu is now the longest-serving prime minister in Israeli history.
